what_it_does: Helps treat acne by reducing excess oil, buildup, and acne-related microbes.
summary_short: Sulfur is mainly used in acne products for its oil-reducing and mild exfoliating effects. It can help dry out blemishes and loosen clogged skin buildup, but it may also feel drying or have a noticeable odor.
summary_long:
Sulfur is an old-school acne ingredient that works mainly as a **keratolytic** and oil-controlling agent. In simpler terms, it helps loosen dead skin buildup inside pores and can make very oily areas feel drier. It also has some antimicrobial activity, which may help explain its use in blemish-focused products.

For acne, sulfur is best understood as a supportive spot-treatment or mask ingredient rather than a modern gold-standard treatment like benzoyl peroxide, salicylic acid, or retinoids. Evidence and long-term data are more limited than for those better-studied acne actives, but sulfur has a long history of use and can be helpful for some people with oily, congested, or inflamed-looking breakouts.

Sulfur is commonly found in cleansers, masks, spot treatments, and medicated acne products. Leave-on acne products often use higher percentages than rinse-off formulas, and product directions matter because overuse can make skin dry, tight, flaky, or irritated.

The main downsides are **dryness, irritation, and smell**. Sensitive, eczema-prone, or already-dry skin may not tolerate sulfur well, especially when layered with other drying actives. Start slowly and avoid using it on the same area as strong exfoliating acids, retinoids, or benzoyl peroxide unless your skin is already well-adjusted.

Sulfur is often paired with ingredients like resorcinol, salicylic acid, clay, zinc, or soothing agents. Hydrating and barrier-supporting ingredients such as glycerin, panthenol, ceramides, or niacinamide can help offset dryness.
quick_facts: Used mostly for acne and oily skin
May smell like sulfur or eggs
